Second-Order Confirmatory Factor Analysis Model

Source: R/fa_second_order.R
fa_second_order.Rd

Fits the second-order factor model, in which first-order factors account for what the items of each subscale share and one or more second-order factors account for what the first-order factors share. The model is described as in fa_confirmatory, by naming the items of each first-order factor, together with the first-order factors of each second-order factor, and is fit by maximum likelihood to raw data (by full information maximum likelihood, the default, or after listwise deletion) or to a covariance matrix. The table reports the first-order and second-order loadings, the error variances, and the intercepts with their confidence intervals; the indices that describe how much of the total score and of each subscale score the second-order factor accounts for: omega and omega hierarchical (omega_H) for the total score, omega and omega hierarchical subscale (omega_HS) for each subscale score, the explained common variance (ECV), coefficient H, and the maximal reliability, each with a delta method standard error and a confidence interval, and the percentage of uncontaminated correlations (PUC), which depends on the structure alone and so has neither; and the fit of the model. The Schmid-Leiman solution the estimates imply (Schmid & Leiman, 1957), the loadings of every item on the second-order factor and on what its first-order factor measures beyond it, is returned as an attribute.

Usage

fa_second_order(
  data = NULL,
  factors,
  second_order,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  M = NULL,
  equal_loading = FALSE,
  equal_intercept = FALSE,
  equal_error = FALSE,
  equal_second_order_loading = FALSE,
  meanstructure = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  se = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9,
  output = c("verbose", "measurement", "summary", "standardized", "fit"),
  ...,
  wald_df = Inf
)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_fa_second_order'
tidy(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_fa_second_order'
glance(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A raw data matrix or data frame, rows are respondents and columns include the items named in factors. Supply exactly one of data or S.

factors

Named list of the first-order factors. Each element names a first-order factor and gives the character vector of its items, two or more; each item is listed under one first-order factor. An item that is not a column of data or an item of S is refused with an error of class dmar_items_invalid (see dmar_metadata).

second_order

Named list of the second-order factors. Each element names a second-order factor and gives the character vector of its first-order factors, named as factors names them; each first-order factor is listed under one second-order factor. One second-order factor needs three or more first-order factors, or two with equal_second_order_loading; with two or more second-order factors, which are always correlated (uncorrelated second-order factors are not offered), two first-order factors each are enough. See Details for the structures that are refused.

S

A symmetric covariance matrix of the items, with dimnames naming the items; N is then required. Supply exactly one of data or S.

N

Total sample size. Required with S; ignored (inferred from the rows) with data.

M

Optional named numeric vector of item means, used with a covariance matrix to model the mean structure (required there when equal_intercept is used). Ignored for raw data.

equal_loading

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per first-order factor. TRUE constrains the loadings of a first-order factor's items to a single value. Defaults to FALSE.

equal_intercept

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per first-order factor. TRUE constrains the intercepts of a first-order factor's items to a single value; this requires the mean structure. Defaults to FALSE.

equal_error

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per first-order factor. TRUE constrains the error variances of a first-order factor's items to a single value. Defaults to FALSE.

equal_second_order_loading

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per second-order factor. TRUE constrains the loadings of a second-order factor's first-order factors to a single value, so that they correlate equally with it. Defaults to FALSE.

meanstructure

Logical or NULL. NULL (default) models the mean structure exactly when it is needed: under FIML (the default with raw data, so the item intercepts, the nu rows, join the table), when any equal_intercept is TRUE, or when M is supplied. TRUE models the intercepts regardless (raw data or M required); FALSE suppresses them, which FIML does not allow.

estimator

"ML" (default), maximum likelihood, or "MLR", maximum likelihood with standard errors and a test statistic robust to nonnormality (raw data required). Ordered items are not available.

missing

The missing data treatment for raw data: "fiml" (default; full information maximum likelihood, which uses every case with an observed item; lavaan's name "ml" is accepted) or "listwise". The default is resolved as in fa_confirmatory: with se = "robust.sem" or a test statistic FIML cannot compute, the items are fit as they stand when no item value is missing, and otherwise the call stops and names the option to choose. Ignored with S.

se

Standard error method passed to lavaan. The default, NULL, follows the estimator: "standard" for ML and "robust.huber.white" for MLR. "robust.sem" requires complete data and is refused with FIML, and "none" requests point estimates only.

conf_level

Confidence level of the intervals for the parameters and the indices. Defaults to 0.95. It does not reach the RMSEA interval, whose level is rmsea_conf_level.

rmsea_conf_level

Confidence level of the RMSEA interval of the fit rows, which the rmsea_ci_level row records. Defaults to 0.90, the conventional level, whose limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see sem_fit_measures); rmsea_conf_level = 0.95 gives a 95 percent interval. It sets the level in the table DMAR returns and in its glance(); output = "summary" returns the lavaan summary, which shows lavaan's 90 percent interval whatever this argument is.

output

Format of the returned object:

"verbose"

(default) The first-order loadings, disturbance variances (fixed at 1), error variances, and intercepts, the second-order loadings, variances (fixed at 1), and correlations, then the indices, then the fit rows.

"measurement"

The indices alone.

"summary"

The summary() of the lavaan fit (not a data frame).

"standardized"

lavaan::standardizedSolution() of the fit, whose rows for the second-order loadings are the correlations of the first-order factors with their second-order factor; the indices are not among its rows (see Details). Under se = "none" its se, z, pvalue, ci.lower, and ci.upper columns are NA.

"fit"

The lavaan fit, which lavaan::lavTestLRT() takes to test the model against the bifactor model (see Details).

...

For fa_second_order(), additional arguments forwarded to lavaan (for example cluster); a group argument is an error, as in fa_confirmatory(), and so is ordered. Unused by tidy() and glance().

wald_df

The reference distribution of the Wald intervals and p-values: Inf (the default), the normal distribution, or a single positive number, the degrees of freedom of a t distribution for every parameter and index row (for the indices, on the logit scale), as in fa_confirmatory. The keyword "missing_information" is refused: the calibration study behind it simulated one factor models, and nothing calibrates it for the loadings of a second-order model or for its indices. It follows ..., so it must be named in full.

x

A dmar_fa_second_order table returned by fa_second_order().

Value

For output = "verbose" (default) and "measurement", a data.frame (classes dmar_fa_second_order, dmar_tbl) with columns syntax, term, estimate, se, test_statistic, p_value, ci_lower, and ci_upper. Its attributes record the model: factors and second_order; equal, a list naming the factors whose loadings, error variances, intercepts, and second-order loadings are equated; has_means; structural_df, the degrees of freedom of the second-order structure (0 when it is just identified); omega_metric ("raw_item_sum"); improper, the negative error variances named by item (empty for a proper solution); improper_second_order, the standardized second-order loadings at one and the second-order correlations beyond one, named by their terms (empty for a proper solution); schmid_leiman, the Schmid-Leiman solution described above; and wald_df. The verbose table also carries fa_confirmatory()'s test, estimator, missing, fit_indices, and fit_rows. The printed header describes the model, and the lines under the table say what the indices describe. For "summary", the lavaan summary; for "standardized", the standardized solution with the "wald_df" attribute; for "fit", the lavaan fit. tidy() gives the parameter and index rows and glance() one row of the fit rows and what produced them, as for fa_confirmatory.

Details

The model is also called the higher-order factor model, and sometimes the hierarchical factor model. The function is named for the structure it fits because Schmid and Leiman (1957) and Yung, Thissen, and McLeod (1999) use "hierarchical factor model" for the other model, the one with uncorrelated factors in layers, of which the bifactor model fit by fa_bifactor is the two-layer case.

The model. An item \(i\) of first-order factor \(f\) is $$x_i = \nu_i + \lambda_i f + e_i,$$ and the first-order factor \(f\) of second-order factor \(g\) is $$f = \gamma_f g + u_f,$$ where the disturbance \(u_f\) is the part of \(f\) that \(g\) does not account for. The model is identified as lavaan's std.lv = TRUE identifies it: the variance of every second-order factor is fixed at 1 (and its mean at 0 when the mean structure is modeled), and so is the variance of every disturbance, so every first-order loading \(\lambda_i\) and every second-order loading \(\gamma_f\) is free. Both constraints are linear. The variance of \(f\) is then \(1 + \gamma_f^2\), and its correlation with \(g\), the standardized second-order loading, is \(\gamma_f / \sqrt{1 + \gamma_f^2}\). Two or more second-order factors are correlated with each other (the phi rows), and the function offers correlated second-order factors only: uncorrelated ones would hold every first-order factor under one second-order factor uncorrelated with every first-order factor under another, and would leave a second-order factor of two first-order factors unidentified (lavaan::cfa() with std.lv = TRUE and orthogonal = TRUE fits that model). A factor fits as well reflected: a first-order factor with every one of its loadings and its second-order loading reversed in sign, a second-order factor with its second-order loadings and its correlations reversed. Each first-order factor is reported in the direction in which its loadings sum to a positive value, and then each second-order factor in the direction in which its second-order loadings do, so a subscale whose items are scored in reverse shows positive loadings and a negative second-order loading. A first-order factor under a second-order factor with equal loadings is not reflected alone, which would break the equality, and keeps the direction the common loading gives it. Should a reflection fail, a warning says so and the factor is reported as the optimizer left it, which changes the signs of its loadings and nothing else. Every loading, error variance, and intercept carries a label, as in fa_confirmatory, and the indices are lavaan defined parameters of those labels, so the fit itself gives each one a delta method standard error. The standardized solution is derived from this fit of the covariances (or of the raw data), not from a fit to correlations.

Scope and identification. A structure outside the model, or one the data cannot identify, is refused before anything is fit, with an error of class dmar_second_order_unidentified (which inherits dmar_refusal; see dmar_metadata) that names the factors or items at issue and gives the kind of refusal as its reason element, as in fa_bifactor. Not identified ("unidentified"): a first-order factor of one item, whose loading cannot be told apart from its error variance; a second-order factor of one first-order factor, which cannot be told apart from it; and one second-order factor over two first-order factors with free loadings, whose one correlation is the product of the two standardized loadings (equal loadings identify them). Outside the model ("scope"): an item under two first-order factors, or a first-order factor under two second-order factors. Names ("names"): an item or a first-order factor listed twice under one factor, a first-order factor under no second-order factor, and names that coincide. The identification checks run once the other arguments and the data have passed theirs. With two or more second-order factors, a second-order factor of two first-order factors is identified through the correlations of its first-order factors with those of the others, and is empirically underidentified when the second-order factors barely correlate. With incomplete raw data under FIML, first-order factors that no case observes together (no case has an item of one and an item of the other) are refused too, as "unidentified", when the pairs of first-order factors the data do observe together do not identify the second-order loadings: three first-order factors under one second-order factor with one pair never observed together leave two correlations for three loadings, while four with one such pair leave five for four and are fit. When lavaan's information matrix cannot be inverted, or is singular, whether it is the observed or the expected information, every standard error, test, and interval is NA, the maximal reliability's included, with a warning, as in fa_bifactor.

A just identified structural part. The second-order loadings and correlations account for the correlations of the first-order factors, \(k(k - 1)/2\) of them for \(k\) first-order factors. Exactly three first-order factors under one second-order factor have three correlations and three second-order loadings, and two with equal loadings have one of each, so the second-order structure is just identified: it is another parameterization of the correlated factors model of the same first-order factors, which fa_confirmatory fits. Whenever that model's three correlations have a positive product and imply standardized second-order loadings below one in absolute value (its one correlation is positive, for two factors), the two models fit exactly alike, with the same chi square on the same degrees of freedom, and the test of fit says nothing about the second-order structure; a line under the table says so, and the structural_df attribute, the correlations less the second-order parameters, is 0. On holzinger_swineford, nine tests in three groups of three (visual perception, cubes, and lozenges; paragraph comprehension, sentence completion, and word meaning; addition, counting groups of dots, and straight and curved capitals) give a chi square of 85.31 on 24 degrees of freedom under both models. Four or more first-order factors leave the second-order structure something to test.

The Schmid-Leiman solution. Substituting the second line of the model into the first gives $$x_i = \nu_i + \lambda_i \gamma_f g + \lambda_i u_f + e_i,$$ a model in which every item loads on the second-order factor and on its first-order factor's disturbance, all of them uncorrelated with variance 1: the transformation of Schmid and Leiman (1957), which turns a second-order solution into one with uncorrelated factors in layers. In the standardized metric an item's loading on \(g\) is \(\lambda^*_i \gamma^*_f\) and its loading on \(u_f\) is \(\lambda^*_i \sqrt{1 - \gamma^{*2}_f}\), with \(\lambda^*_i\) its standardized first-order loading and \(\gamma^*_f\) the standardized second-order loading of its factor (Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999, Eqs. 4 and 10). These are the general_loading and group_loading columns of the schmid_leiman attribute, beside item, factor (the first-order factor), second_order, and uniqueness, one minus the sum of their squares. Within a first-order factor the ratio of the two loadings is \(\gamma^*_f / \sqrt{1 - \gamma^{*2}_f}\) for every item: the proportionality constraint by which the second-order model differs from a bifactor model with the same groups, whose general and group loadings are free (Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999; Chen, West, & Sousa, 2006).

The indices. The indices are those of fa_bifactor, computed from the Schmid-Leiman loadings of the items of each second-order factor: in the unstandardized metric, the general loading \(\lambda_i \gamma_f\) and the group loading \(\lambda_i\), beside the error variance \(\psi_i\), with model implied item variance \(v_i = \lambda_i^2 (1 + \gamma_f^2) + \psi_i\). The variance of the total score, the unweighted sum of the items of a second-order factor \(g\), is $$\sigma^2_X = (\textstyle\sum_i \lambda_i \gamma_{f(i)})^2 + \sum_f (\sum_{i \in f} \lambda_i)^2 + \sum_i \psi_i,$$ and the rows are

omega_<g>

Omega for the total score, the share of \(\sigma^2_X\) that is not error variance: its reliability with every factor counted as true score.

omega_H_<g>

Omega hierarchical, \((\sum_i \lambda_i \gamma_{f(i)})^2 / \sigma^2_X\): the share of the total score's variance that is due to the second-order factor alone.

omega_<f>

Omega for the subscale score of first-order factor \(f\), the sum of its items, \((\sum_{i \in f} \lambda_i)^2 (1 + \gamma_f^2)\) over that score's variance, which adds \(\sum_{i \in f} \psi_i\): the omega that fa_confirmatory reports for a factor, here at the estimates of the second-order model.

omega_HS_<f>

Omega hierarchical subscale, \((\sum_{i \in f} \lambda_i)^2\) over the same variance: the share of the subscale score's variance that is due to the disturbance of \(f\), what the subscale score says beyond the second-order factor.

ECV_<g>, ECV_<f>

The explained common variance, formed from the standardized Schmid-Leiman loadings as fa_bifactor forms it: for \(g\), its share of the common variance of its items; for \(f\), the share of the common variance of the items of \(f\) that is due to \(g\), which in this model is \(\gamma^{*2}_f\), the squared standardized second-order loading, since every item of \(f\) divides its common variance in that proportion.

H_<g>, H_<f>

Coefficient H in the form of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016), the closed form of Hancock and Mueller (2001) over the factor's Schmid-Leiman loadings with every other source of an item's variance counted as its error.

maximal_reliability_<g>, maximal_reliability_<f>

The maximal reliability under the fitted model, \(c' \Sigma^{-1} c\), with \(c\) the covariances of all of the items with the factor and \(\Sigma\) their model implied covariance matrix: the largest reliability any weighted sum of the items reaches as a measure of \(g\), or of the disturbance of \(f\). With several second-order factors, the items of the others count too, through the correlations of the second-order factors.

PUC_<g>

The percentage of uncontaminated correlations, as a proportion: the share of the pairs of the items of \(g\) that do not share a first-order factor. It depends on the structure, not on the data, so it has no standard error or interval.

With several second-order factors each one's rows describe the sum of its own items. Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) describe how each index is read; the table reports the numbers with their uncertainty, and whether a total or subscale score is worth reporting is the researcher's judgment, on which the package draws no line. Omega, omega_H, and omega_HS describe unit-weighted sums of the items as they are scored, as in fa_bifactor; ECV, H, the maximal reliability, and PUC do not depend on the metric of the items. With output = "standardized", lavaan would evaluate the defined indices at the standardized values of their labels, and a standardized first-order loading is scaled by the whole variance of its factor, not by that of the disturbance the indices need, so the index rows are left out of that output, and lavaan's warning that under equal_loading or equal_error their standardized values are ambiguous is not passed on.

Intervals. As in fa_bifactor: the standard errors of omega, omega_H, omega_HS, ECV, and H are lavaan's delta method standard errors of the defined parameters, that of the maximal reliability is the delta method's with the derivatives taken numerically, and the limits of every index are formed on the logit scale from that standard error and transformed back (Browne, 1982; the confidence interval transformation principle of Kelley, 2007), so they lie within (0, 1); the se column is the standard error of the index itself.

The test against the bifactor model. The second-order model is nested in the bifactor model whose group factors are its first-order factors: the bifactor model frees the proportionality constraint above (Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999; Chen, West, & Sousa, 2006). With output = "fit" from both functions, lavaan::lavTestLRT(fa_second_order(..., output = "fit"), fa_bifactor(..., output = "fit")) gives the likelihood ratio test of the constraint, on as many degrees of freedom as there are items less first-order factors (Yung, Thissen, & McLeod, 1999), as the example shows. When the second-order structure is just identified the second-order fit is that of the correlated factors model, and the test compares the bifactor model with it. The comparison is for one second-order factor; the bifactor model of fa_bifactor has one general factor.

Finding the maximum. In the parameterization above a standardized second-order loading reaches one only as \(\gamma_f\) runs off to infinity, the loadings \(\lambda_i\) of its factor shrinking toward zero beside it, and lavaan's optimizer can stop on the way at a point that is not the maximum of the likelihood, with other second-order loadings drifted far from their values there, or fail to converge. The function therefore fits the model a second time, in a parameterization that writes each first-order factor on the scale of its second-order factor, \(f = g + u_f\), with the variance of \(u_f\), which is \(1 / \gamma_f^2\), free and bounded below at zero, so that a standardized loading of one is a point the optimizer reaches; the equality constraints of the call hold exactly in it, as in the first. That fit starts from the first and, when the first did not converge, came near the boundary, or fell short, also from lavaan's own starting values; the largest log likelihood is carried back to the parameterization above, so the estimates and the fit rows are those of the maximum, and lavaan accepts each fit only where its gradient is near zero. Log likelihoods are compared per case (two within 1e-6 per case are taken to be the same maximum), since the log likelihood is a sum over the cases and the comparison should not depend on their number. On holzinger_swineford, one second-order factor over the spatial, verbal, and speed tests of the example and the three tests with missing values (t24_woody_mccall, t25_paper_form_board_r, and t26_flags) stopped at a chi square of 251.77 in the first parameterization, with three second-order loadings between 43 and 233; the maximum is 169.77. When the second fit cannot be made, a warning says that the maximum could not be confirmed and names any standardized second-order loading of .995 or more as possibly a point where the optimizer stopped; when neither fit converges, the error says so and names the standardized second-order loadings the first fit was taking toward one.

Improper solutions. As in fa_bifactor, a negative error variance makes the maximal reliabilities undefined, and with them the H of a factor on which an item's standardized Schmid-Leiman loading reaches one and an omega whose items' error variances sum below zero; those rows are NA, with a warning that names the items (beside the warning of class dmar_heywood_warning that fa_confirmatory gives), and the improper attribute holds the negative error variances. When the likelihood has no maximum at all, flat or still rising as an error variance falls, the function stops for every output, as fa_bifactor does, with an error of class dmar_no_maximum that prints the lavaan code of the fit (with a standardized second-order loading at one, that of the second fit described above, in which the check is made); there, bounds = "pos.var" or a different model are the choices. The second order has improper solutions of its own, handled in the same way. A standardized second-order loading of one, a Heywood case at the second order, leaves the first-order factor's disturbance without variance (a parameterization that let that variance be negative would estimate it at or below zero). The loading is at one when the second fit above puts the variance of \(u_f\) at its bound of zero (within 1e-6 of it, a standardized loading of .9999995 or more). The parameterization above has no point there, so the fit holds the loading within 5e-9 of one, where the log likelihood is within 1e-6 per case of its maximum, and that factor's second-order loading and its loadings on its disturbance have no finite estimate and are NA, as are the rows of its disturbance, omega_HS, ECV, H, and the maximal reliability of that first-order factor. The other rows are those of the maximum, their standard errors computed with the loading held at one (with se = "bootstrap" they are NA, with a warning, since the fit at that point is computed without the optimizer and a bootstrap of it would not refit the samples); the fit rows are those of the model at its maximum, on its own degrees of freedom; and the factor's items have group loadings of zero in the Schmid-Leiman attribute. With output = "fit", "summary", or "standardized" the object holds the loading at that point, and a warning says so; with se = "bootstrap" that object carries no standard errors, tests, or intervals (lavaan's se = "none"). Under FIML, lavaan cannot form its robust CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and GFI for a fit computed at that point, so the "summary" output shows them as NA, with one warning in place of lavaan's. A correlation of two second-order factors beyond one in absolute value, which leaves the covariance matrix of the latent variables short of positive definite, leaves every maximal reliability NA, since each reads that correlation. A warning names the factors, and the improper_second_order attribute holds the standardized loadings at one and the correlations beyond one, named by their terms. Two second-order factors over two or three first-order factors each are prone to both: of the ten ways of placing five first-order factors of holzinger_swineford (spatial, verbal, speed, memory, and reasoning tests), two under one second-order factor and three under the other, every one puts the standardized second-order loading of the reasoning factor at one, and seven of them also give a correlation of the second-order factors beyond one.

Ordered items. fa_second_order() fits continuous items, and ordered is refused.

Row names under term: lambda_<factor>_<j> (first-order loadings, numbered within the factor; lambda_<factor> when equated), zeta_<factor> (the disturbance variances, fixed at 1), psi_<factor>_<j> and nu_<factor>_<j> (the error variances and intercepts), gamma_<second>_<factor> (second-order loadings; gamma_<second> when equated), phi_<second> (the second-order variances, fixed at 1), phi_<second>_<second> (the correlations of the second-order factors), the indices above, and fa_confirmatory's fit rows chi_square through H1, whose versions and the lines under the table are as there.

References

Browne, M. W. (1982). Covariance structures. In D. M. Hawkins (Ed.), Topics in applied multivariate analysis (pp. 72–141). Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press.

Chen, F. F., West, S. G., & Sousa, K. H. (2006). A comparison of bifactor and second-order models of quality of life. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 41(2), 189–225. doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr4102_5

Hancock, G. R., & Mueller, R. O. (2001). Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In R. Cudeck, S. du Toit, & D. Sörbom (Eds.), Structural equation modeling: Present and future (pp. 195–216). Scientific Software International.

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. doi:10.1037/met0000045

Schmid, J., & Leiman, J. M. (1957). The development of hierarchical factor solutions. Psychometrika, 22(1), 53–61. doi:10.1007/BF02289209

Yung, Y.-F., Thissen, D., & McLeod, L. D. (1999). On the relationship between the higher-order factor model and the hierarchical factor model. Psychometrika, 64(2), 113–128. doi:10.1007/BF02294531

See also

fa_bifactor for the bifactor model of the same groups, in which the second-order model is nested; fa_confirmatory for the correlated factors model of the first-order factors; reliability_omega and reliability_H.

Examples

data(holzinger_swineford)
hs_factors <- list(
  spatial = c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges"),
  verbal  = c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",
              "t9_word_meaning"),
  speed   = c("t10_addition", "t12_counting_groups_of_dots",
              "t13_straight_and_curved_capitals"),
  memory  = c("t14_word_recognition", "t15_number_recognition",
              "t17_object_number"))
hs_second <- list(general = c("spatial", "verbal", "speed", "memory"))

# One second-order factor over four first-order factors: the indices,
# each with a delta method interval.
so <- fa_second_order(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, hs_second,
                      output = "measurement")
so
#> Second-order model: general over spatial (3 items), verbal (3 items), speed (3 items), memory (3 items)
#> Every second-order factor's variance and every first-order factor's disturbance variance is fixed at 1
#> 
#>  syntax term                        estimate se    test_statistic p_value

#> omega, omega_H, and omega_HS describe unit-weighted sums of the items as scored; ECV, H, and maximal_reliability are formed from the Schmid-Leiman loadings (attribute schmid_leiman) and do not depend on the metric of the items; PUC depends on the structure alone, so it has no interval
#> 
#> For a first-order factor, omega is the reliability of the total score of its items, omega_HS the share of that score's variance due to the factor's disturbance (what the second-order factor does not account for), ECV the second-order factor's share of the items' common variance, and H and maximal_reliability describe the disturbance

# The Schmid-Leiman loadings the estimates imply.
attr(so, "schmid_leiman")

# The second-order model is the bifactor model of the same groups with
# the general loadings proportional to the group loadings; the
# likelihood ratio test of that constraint, on 12 - 4 = 8 degrees of
# freedom.
second_order_fit <- fa_second_order(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors,
                                    hs_second, output = "fit")
bifactor_fit <- fa_bifactor(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors,
                            output = "fit")
print_anova(lavaan::lavTestLRT(second_order_fit, bifactor_fit))
